20|BACKGROUND
21|Darolutamide is a potent androgen-receptor inhibitor that has been associated
22|with increased overall survival among patients with nonmetastatic, castration-
23|resistant prostate cancer. Whether a combination of darolutamide, androgen-
24|deprivation therapy, and docetaxel would increase survival among patients with
25|metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is unknown.
26|METHODS
27|In this international, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with meta-
28|static, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a 1:1 ratio to receive darolutamide (at
29|a dose of 600 mg [two 300-mg tablets] twice daily) or matching placebo, both in
30|combination with androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel. The primary end
31|point was overall survival.
32|RESULTS
33|The primary analysis involved 1306 patients (651 in the darolutamide group and
34|655 in the placebo group); 86.1% of the patients had disease that was metastatic
35|at the time of the initial diagnosis. At the data cutoff date for the primary analysis
36|(October 25, 2021), the risk of death was significantly lower, by 32.5%, in the
37|darolutamide group than in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% confidence
38|interval, 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001). Darolutamide was also associated with consistent
39|benefits with respect to the secondary end points and prespecified subgroups.
40|Adverse events were similar in the two groups, and the incidences of the most
41|common adverse events (occurring in ≥10% of the patients) were highest during
42|the overlapping docetaxel treatment period in both groups. The frequency of grade
43|3 or 4 adverse events was 66.1% in the darolutamide group and 63.5% in the pla-
44|cebo group; neutropenia was the most common grade 3 or 4 adverse event (in
45|33.7% and 34.2%, respectively).
46|CONCLUSIONS
47|In this trial involving patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer,
48|overall survival was significantly longer with the combination of darolutamide,
49|androgen-deprivation therapy, and docetaxel than with placebo plus androgen-
50|deprivation therapy and docetaxel, and the addition of darolutamide led to improve-
51|ment in key secondary end points. The frequency of adverse events was similar in
52|the two groups. (Funded by Bayer and Orion Pharma; ARASENS ClinicalTrials.gov
53|number, NCT02799602.)

3|Darolutamide in Metastatic Prostate Cancer
4|S
5|tandard treatment for patients
6|with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
7|tate cancer includes the addition of either
8|docetaxel or an androgen-receptor pathway in-
9|hibitor to androgen-deprivation therapy.1-4 In two
10|randomized, phase 3 trials involving such pa-
11|tients, overall survival was longer among those
12|who received docetaxel plus androgen-depriva-
13|tion therapy than among those who received
14|androgen-deprivation therapy alone.5-8 Subsequent
15|randomized, phase 3 trials have shown that the
16|addition of an androgen-receptor pathway inhibi-
17|tor (abiraterone, enzalutamide, or apalutamide)
18|to androgen-deprivation therapy has greater clini-
19|cal benefit than the use of androgen-deprivation
20|therapy alone.9-12
21|Phase 3 trials of combination therapy with an
22|androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor, androgen-
23|deprivation therapy, and docetaxel have shown
24|conflicting results. In PEACE-1 (A Phase III
25|Study for Patients with Metastatic Hormone-
26|naïve Prostate Cancer), overall survival was longer
27|among patients who received abiraterone in
28|combination with androgen-deprivation therapy
29|and docetaxel than among those who received
30|androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel
31|alone.13 In contrast, a subgroup analysis of the
32|ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First Line Andro-
33|gen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic Prostate
34|Cancer) trial showed that survival was not longer
35|with enzalutamide, androgen-deprivation ther-
36|apy, and docetaxel than with androgen-depriva-
37|tion therapy and docetaxel alone.12
38|Darolutamide is a structurally distinct andro-
39|gen-receptor inhibitor with low blood-brain bar-
40|rier penetration and limited potential for clini-
41|cally relevant drug-drug interactions.14-17 Studies
42|involving patients with prostate cancer, includ-
43|ing the phase 3 ARAMIS (Androgen Receptor
44|Antagonizing Agent for Metastasis-free Survival)
45|trial involving patients with nonmetastatic, cas-
46|tration-resistant prostate cancer, have shown that
47|darolutamide has potent antitumor efficacy.18-22
48|In the ARAMIS trial, the median metastasis-free
49|survival was almost 2 years longer and the risk
50|of death was 31% lower among patients who
51|received darolutamide with androgen-deprivation
52|therapy than among those who received placebo
53|with androgen-deprivation therapy, and the inci-
54|dence of adverse events was similar in the two
55|groups.21,22 In the phase 3 ARASENS (ODM-201
56|in Addition to Standard ADT and Docetaxel in
57|Metastatic Castration Sensitive Prostate Cancer)
58|trial, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of
59|darolutamide added to androgen-deprivation
60|therapy and docetaxel in patients with meta-
61|static, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
62|Methods
63|Trial Design and Conduct
64|This international, randomized, double-blind,
65|placebo-controlled trial was sponsored by Bayer
66|and Orion Pharma. The trial was designed by
67|Bayer and the first and last authors, with sup-
68|port from the protocol steering committee. The
69|institutional review board at each participating
70|institution approved the trial, which was con-
71|ducted in accordance with the principles of the
72|Declaration of Helsinki and the International
73|Council for Harmonisation Good Clinical Prac-
74|tice guidelines. All the patients provided written
75|informed consent.
76|An independent data and safety monitoring
77|board reviewed unblinded safety and efficacy
78|data throughout the trial. The data were col-
79|lected by the investigators, analyzed by statisti-
80|cians who were employed by Bayer, and inter-
81|preted by the authors, including employees of
82|the sponsors. Bayer provided funding for medi-
83|cal writing assistance. All the authors reviewed
84|and approved the manuscript that was submitted
85|for publication. The authors assume responsibil-
86|ity for the completeness and accuracy of the data
87|and for the fidelity of the trial to the protocol
88|and the statistical analysis plan, available with
89|the full text of this article at NEJM.org.
90|Patients and Interventions
91|Patients were eligible for participation if they
92|were 18 years of age or older and had an Eastern
93|Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) perfor-
94|mance-status score of 0 or 1 (scores range from
95|0 to 5, with higher scores indicating greater dis-
96|ability), histologically or cytologically confirmed
97|prostate cancer, and metastases detected on bone
98|scanning, contrast-enhanced computed tomog-
99|raphy (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging
100|(MRI). Eligible patients had to be candidates for
101|androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel, in
102|the investigator's judgment. Patients were ex-
103|cluded if they had regional lymph-node involve-
104|ment only (N1, below the aortic bifurcation) or
105|if they had received androgen-deprivation ther-
106|apy more than 12 weeks before randomization,
107|second-generation androgen-receptor pathway

7|Full eligibility criteria are provided in the Sup-
8|plementary Appendix, available at NEJM.org.
9|All the patients received androgen-depriva-
10|tion therapy (a luteinizing hormone-releasing
11|hormone [LHRH] agonist or an LHRH antago-
12|nist) or underwent orchiectomy within 12 weeks
13|before randomization and received six cycles of
14|docetaxel (75 mg per square meter of body-sur-
15|face area on day 1 and every 21 days), with pred-
16|nisone or prednisolone administered at the in-
17|vestigator's discretion, initiated within 6 weeks
18|after randomization. The recommended pre-
19|medication to prevent docetaxel-related hyper-
20|sensitivity reactions and fluid retention was oral
21|dexamethasone, administered at a dose of 8 mg
22|at 12 hours, 3 hours, and 1 hour before infusion.
23|For patients receiving LHRH agonists, the use of
24|these agonists in combination with a first-gen-
25|eration antiandrogen for at least 4 weeks before
26|randomization was recommended. First-genera-
27|tion antiandrogen therapy was discontinued be-
28|fore randomization.
29|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
30|to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
31|[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
32|matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
33|according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
34|node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
35|metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
36|without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
37|ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
38|bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
39|er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
40|or above the upper limit of the normal range.
41|Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
42|placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
43|a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
44|toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
45|or nonadherence.
46|End Points
47|The primary end point was overall survival,
48|which was defined as the time from randomiza-
49|tion until death from any cause. The secondary
50|end points were time to castration-resistant
51|prostate cancer, time to pain progression, symp-
52|tomatic skeletal event-free survival, time to a
53|first symptomatic skeletal event, time to initia-
54|tion of subsequent systemic antineoplastic ther-
55|apy, time to worsening of disease-related physi-
56|cal symptoms, time to initiation of opioid
57|treatment for 7 or more consecutive days, and
58|safety. Definitions of the secondary efficacy
59|end points are provided in the Supplementary
60|Appendix.
61|Assessments
62|During the trial, patients were evaluated every
63|12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
64|the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
65|apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
66|7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
67|the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
68|and adverse events and serious adverse events
69|that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
70|went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
71|vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
72|within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
73|and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
74|was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
75|ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
76|related physical symptoms were assessed with
77|the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
78|Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
79|cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
80|naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
81|graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
82|stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
83|Events, version 4.03.
84|Statistical Analysis
85|The sample size was calculated on the basis of
86|the primary end point, overall survival. We esti-
87|mated that approximately 1300 patients would
88|be required to observe approximately 509 deaths,
89|allowing for a 5% dropout rate, which would
90|provide the trial with 90% power to detect a 25%
91|decrease in the risk of death in the darolutamide
92|group versus the placebo group, at a two-sided
93|alpha level of 0.05. The secondary end points
94|were tested with a hierarchical gatekeeping pro-
95|cedure in the order described above only if the
96|primary end point and each preceding secondary
97|end point in the hierarchy were statistically sig-
98|nificant. If the primary end point or a secondary
99|end point did not reach significance, the hierar-
100|chical procedure was stopped, and subsequent
101|analyses were considered to be exploratory.

7|mary and secondary efficacy end points with the
8|use of a stratified log-rank test, with randomiza-
9|tion stratification factors. Hazard ratios for the
10|comparison of darolutamide with placebo and
11|95% confidence intervals were calculated with
12|the Cox proportional-hazards model stratified
13|according to the randomization factors. A log-
14|log survival plot, which was produced to assess
15|whether application of the Cox proportional-
16|hazards model was appropriate, confirmed that
17|the proportional-hazards assumption was met
18|for all time-to-event end points. Kaplan-Meier
19|estimates for overall survival are presented for
20|both treatment groups. For the analysis of over-
21|all survival, data on patients in whom death had
22|not been confirmed were censored as of the last
23|known date the patients were alive. For sub-
24|group analyses, intervals were not adjusted for
25|multiplicity and cannot be used to infer effects.
26|Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
27|baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
28|and safety end points were assessed in the safety
29|analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
30|least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
31|were assessed in accordance with the treatment
32|that they actually received). For the primary effi-
33|cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
34|fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
35|fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
36|use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
37|Results
38|Patients
39|Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
40|of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
41|286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
42|tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
43|655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
44|both in combination with androgen-deprivation
45|therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
46|the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
47|1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
48|and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
49|the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
50|the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
51|group) were included in the safety analysis set.
52|Demographic and baseline characteristics
53|were well balanced in the two groups (Tables 1
54|and S2). The median age was 67 years in both
55|groups, most patients (71.1%) had an ECOG
56|performance-status score of 0, and 78.2% of the
57|patients had a Gleason score of 8 or greater
58|(scores range from 6 to 10, with higher scores
59|indicating a more aggressive form of prostate
60|cancer). All the patients had metastatic disease
61|at baseline; 79.5% had bone metastases (metas-
62|tasis stage M1b) and 17.5% had visceral me-
63|tastases (metastasis stage M1c). Most patients
64|(86.1%) had disease that was metastatic at the
65|time of the initial diagnosis.
66|At the data cutoff date for the primary analy-
67|sis (October 25, 2021), the median treatment
68|duration was longer in the darolutamide group
69|(41.0 months) than in the placebo group (16.7
70|months), and a higher percentage of patients in
71|the darolutamide group (45.9% [299 of 651 pa-
72|tients]) than in the placebo group (19.1% [125 of
73|654 patients]) were still receiving the assigned
74|trial treatment. Six cycles of docetaxel were
75|completed in 571 of 652 patients (87.6%) in the
76|darolutamide group and in 556 of 650 patients
77|(85.5%) in the placebo group. The reasons for
78|discontinuation of the trial agent are provided in
79|Figure S1. The median follow-up for overall sur-
80|vival was 43.7 months in the darolutamide group
81|and 42.4 months in the placebo group.
82|Primary End Point
83|The primary analysis of overall survival was per-
84|formed after 533 patients had died (229 patients
85|in the darolutamide group and 304 patients in
86|the placebo group). The risk of death was 32.5%
87|lower in the darolutamide group than in the
88|placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.68; 95% confi-
89|dence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001) (Fig. 1).
90|A significant improvement in overall survival was
91|observed despite a high percentage of patients
92|who received subsequent life-prolonging systemic
93|therapies, primarily different androgen-receptor
94|pathway inhibitors, among those who entered
95|follow-up in the placebo group (374 of 495 pa-
96|tients [75.6%]) (Table S3). The overall survival at
97|4 years was 62.7% (95% CI, 58.7 to 66.7) in the
98|darolutamide group and 50.4% (95% CI, 46.3 to
99|54.6) in the placebo group. The treatment effect
100|of darolutamide with respect to overall survival
101|was favorable across most subgroups (Figs. S2
102|and S3).

9|Certain adverse events are of special interest
10|for patients receiving androgen-receptor path-
11|way inhibitors. These events include fatigue,
12|falls, fractures, mental impairment, rash, hyper-
13|tension, and cardiovascular events. In this trial,
14|the incidences of these events of interest were
15|similar (with no more than a 2 percentage-point
16|difference) in the two groups, with the exception
17|of rash (in 16.6% of the patients in the darolu-
18|tamide group and 13.5% of those in the placebo
19|group) and hypertension (in 13.7% and 9.2%,
20|respectively) (Table S6). Among the most fre-
21|quently reported adverse events of interest, the
22|incidences of vasodilation and flushing (in
23|20.4% of the patients in the darolutamide group
24|and 21.7% of those in the placebo group) and
25|diabetes mellitus and hyperglycemia (in 15.2%
26|and 14.3%) were also similar in the two groups.
27|Discussion
28|In this international, randomized, double-blind,
29|placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial involving pa-
30|tients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
31|tate cancer, overall survival was significantly
32|longer among patients who received darolutamide
33|plus androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel
34|than among those who received androgen-depri-
35|vation therapy and docetaxel alone. This survival
36|benefit was observed despite a high percentage
37|of patients who received subsequent life-pro-
38|longing systemic therapy in the placebo group.
39|The survival benefit of darolutamide was consis-
40|tent across most subgroups. The time to the
41|development of castration-resistant disease was
42|significantly longer in the patients who received
43|darolutamide, and improvements were observed
44|with respect to the other key secondary end
45|points. The incidence, severity, and nature of
46|adverse events were consistent with the estab-
47|lished safety profiles of androgen-deprivation
48|therapy and docetaxel.
49|Our results are consistent with those in the
50|PEACE-1 trial, which had a two-by-two factorial
51|design. In that trial, 1173 patients with hormone-
52|sensitive prostate cancer that was metastatic at
53|the time of the initial diagnosis were randomly
54|assigned to receive abiraterone, prostate radio-
55|therapy, neither, or both. All the patients re-
56|ceived standard of care (androgen-deprivation
57|therapy with or without docetaxel). In a planned
58|subgroup analysis involving 710 patients who
59|received docetaxel, overall survival was signifi-
60|cantly longer among those who received abi-
61|raterone than among those who did not (hazard
62|ratio, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.96).13
63|All the patients in the ARASENS trial were
64|prospectively assigned to receive androgen-depri-
65|vation therapy and docetaxel. This trial provided
66|clear and compelling evidence that overall sur-
67|vival was significantly longer among patients
68|who received combination therapy with daroluta
69|mide, androgen-deprivation therapy, and docetax-
70|el than among those who received androgen-
71|deprivation therapy and docetaxel alone.
72|Darolutamide was associated with a 32.5% re-
73|duction in the risk of death. The combination
74|did not result in more toxic effects than did the
75|combination of androgen-deprivation therapy and
76|docetaxel alone. In both the phase 3 ARAMIS
77|trial involving patients with nonmetastatic, castra-
78|tion-resistant prostate cancer and the ARASENS
79|trial, there was no more than a 2 percentage-
80|point difference between the darolutamide and
81|placebo groups with respect to the incidence of
82|most adverse events that are commonly associ-
83|ated with androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors.22
84|This trial has several strengths and limita-
85|tions. The large sample size enabled us to con-
86|duct a robust statistical analysis to assess the
87|effect of the addition of darolutamide, an andro-
88|gen-receptor pathway inhibitor, to androgen-
89|deprivation therapy and docetaxel on overall
90|survival and a number of key secondary end
91|points. Most patients who were enrolled in our
92|trial had metastatic disease, with bone metasta-
93|ses, visceral metastases, or both, at the time of
94|the initial diagnosis. Thus, limited information
95|is available on the benefit-risk considerations
96|for patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive
97|prostate cancer and a better prognosis, includ-
98|ing those with recurrent metastatic disease, node-
99|only metastases, or both. In addition, the effi-
100|cacy and safety of combination therapy are
101|unknown in patients with a poor performance
102|status, because the trial included only patients
103|with an ECOG performance-status score of 0 or 1.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

sections.excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.

evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
and safety end points were assessed in the safety
analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
were assessed in accordance with the treatment
that they actually received). For the primary effi-
cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
Results
Patients
Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
both in combination with androgen-deprivation
therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
group) were included in the safety analysis set.

Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.

Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.

8|At the end of the screening period, all subjects meeting all of the inclusion criteria and none
9|of the exclusion criteria will be randomly assigned on a 1:1 basis in a blinded fashion to
10|treatment with darolutamide or matching placebo plus ADT and docetaxel. In addition,
11|randomization will be stratified by:

23|o

26|ALP≥ULN
27|Note: Blood samples to measure ALP levels for stratification will be analyzed in a central
28|laboratory.
29|A computer-generated randomization list will be prepared by the Bayer Randomization
30|Manager. The randomization number will be used to link the subject to a treatment group and
31|to a medication package.
32|The Investigator (or designated associate) will obtain the randomization number and the
33|medication package numbers assigned to a subject by accessing the Interactive Voice/Web
34|Response System (IXRS) after confirming that the subject meets all the inclusion criteria and
35|does not meet any of the exclusion criteria.
36|An IXRS description and handbook will be provided to each investigational site.
37|7.4
38|Dosage and administration of study treatment
39|7.4.1
40|Dose modifications of study drug
41|The study drug will be administered as oral 300 mg tablets. The dose of study drug to be
42|administered is 600 mg (2 tablets of 300 mg) twice daily with food, equivalent to a total daily
43|dose of 1200 mg. Placebo matching darolutamide tablets in appearance will be administered
44|twice daily with food.
45|The dose or dosing schedule of the study drug may be modified following the occurrence of
46|clinically significant AEs. Doses of study drug may be delayed or reduced in case of clinically
47|significant toxicities that are considered by the Investigator to be related to study drug.
48|Toxicities will be graded using the National Cancer Institute-Common Terminology Criteria
49|for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) v 4.03. All dose modifications regardless of relatedness
50|should be recorded on the eCRF. If a subject experiences several study drug-related toxicities
51|with different grading, the recommendation of the worst grading should be used.

answers.justification: The protocol explicitly states that the Bayer Randomization Manager will prepare a computer-generated randomization list, establishing a random component in sequence generation.

The protocol says the investigator obtains the randomization number and medication package through the Interactive Voice/Web Response System only after confirming eligibility. This centrally administered allocation process supports concealment until enrollment and assignment.

The baseline table shows similar randomized group sizes and broadly comparable characteristics, including ECOG status, metastasis stage, and ALP category. Differences are modest and do not indicate a randomization problem.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Neutral contrast: protocol-permitted rescue after progression is ordinary subsequent care; prohibited rescue encouraged by trial staff is a candidate trial-context deviation. Change only the protocol-consistency and cause premises before changing the reasoning.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
and safety end points were assessed in the safety
analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
were assessed in accordance with the treatment
that they actually received). For the primary effi-
cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
Results
Patients
Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
both in combination with androgen-deprivation
therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
group) were included in the safety analysis set.

Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.

Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
and safety end points were assessed in the safety
analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
were assessed in accordance with the treatment
that they actually received). For the primary effi-
cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
Results
Patients
Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
both in combination with androgen-deprivation
therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
group) were included in the safety analysis set.

Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.

Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.

item.text: For missing outcome data, the report gives safety denominators of 652 and 650 and identifies the three randomized participants who never received treatment; a fourth participant was analyzed in the group corresponding to treatment received. I’m treating the near complete safety set as probably sufficient for this common adverse-event outcome, while noting that the report does not provide separate counts of unrecorded AE assessments.

answers.justification: The AE table provides outcome counts for the safety set of 652 darolutamide and 650 placebo recipients. The report states safety outcomes were assessed for everyone receiving at least one dose, and AE/serious AE assessments occurred during treatment every 12 weeks. Only three randomized placebo participants never received treatment; the table footnote identifies one additional participant assigned to placebo but treated with darolutamide and included with darolutamide. Thus the reported outcome covers nearly all randomized participants, though three have no safety-set outcome and one is attributed by treatment received.
unknowns: The report does not separately state whether any treated participant had an unrecorded AE assessment.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.

This asks only whether the relevant assessor knew assignment. It does not establish that the measurement was susceptible to bias, that detection opportunities differed, or that knowledge likely changed the assessment; those are separate questions.

considerations: Assess whether knowledge could influence this outcome. Evidence that influence actually occurred belongs to 4.5; its absence does not resolve 4.4.

Possible influence requires a judgement or reporting pathway through which assessor awareness could matter. Awareness alone is not a measurement difference, and a susceptible outcome does not by itself show that influence was possible in this assessment.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize
baseline characteristics in the full analysis set,
and safety end points were assessed in the safety
analysis set (i.e., all the patients who received at
least one dose of darolutamide or placebo and
were assessed in accordance with the treatment
that they actually received). For the primary effi-
cacy end point, subgroup analyses were prespeci-
fied to assess the consistency of treatment ef-
fect. Statistical analyses were performed with the
use of SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute).
Results
Patients
Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
both in combination with androgen-deprivation
therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
group) were included in the safety analysis set.

Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.

Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.

questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish source creation/version and amendment dates from trial events and retrieval time; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An embedded SAP can be applicable evidence when its comparison, cohort, and Result fields match; an absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data; a source creation date, registry posting or update date, amendment date, or retrieval date is not automatically the relevant trial chronology.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent, and a data cutoff is not investigator unblinding. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; pre-unblinding finalization differs from ambiguous chronology only in the timing premise.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.

A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.

Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

both in combination with androgen-deprivation
therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
group) were included in the safety analysis set.

Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
or above the upper limit of the normal range.
Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
or nonadherence.

Assessments
During the trial, patients were evaluated every
12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
and adverse events and serious adverse events
that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
related physical symptoms were assessed with
the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
Events, version 4.03.

4|The concentration-time courses of all analytes will be tabulated separated by treatment and

6|arithmetic mean, SD, and coefficient of variation (CV); geometric mean, geometric SD (re-
7|transformed SD of the logarithms), and CV; minimum, median, maximum value, and the
8|number of measurements.
9|Means at any time will only be calculated if at least 2/3 of the individual data were measured
10|and were above the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ). For the calculation of the mean
11|value, a data point below LLOQ will be substituted by one-half of this limit.
12|In tables showing mean values, where values below LLOQ are included in the calculation of
13|mean values, these means will be marked.

6|Design overview
7|This is an international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter Phase III
8|study of darolutamide in patients with mHSPC. Approximately 1,300 patients will be
9|randomized (1:1 ratio) to receive one of the following study drugs:
10|
11|Darolutamide, 600 mg (2 x 300 mg tablets) bid orally with food
12|
13|Placebo matching darolutamide tablets in appearance, bid orally with food
14|All patients must receive ADT of Investigator's choice (LHRH agonist/antagonists or
15|orchiectomy) as standard therapy, started ≤12 weeks before randomization. Six cycles of
16|docetaxel will be administered as background treatment after randomization. The first cycle of
17|docetaxel should be administered within 6 weeks after start of study drug.
18|For at least the first 20 randomized patients who have received at least 1 cycle of docetaxel,
19|and for whom a detailed mandatory PK analysis will be performed, docetaxel should be
20|administered at least 14 days after randomization.

33|o

47|of 1:1 to treatment with darolutamide or placebo.

7.3
Treatment assignment
At the end of the screening period, all subjects meeting all of the inclusion criteria and none
of the exclusion criteria will be randomly assigned on a 1:1 basis in a blinded fashion to
treatment with darolutamide or matching placebo plus ADT and docetaxel. In addition,
randomization will be stratified by:

Extent of disease
o
Non-regional lymph nodes metastases only
o
Bone metastases with or without lymph node metastases
o
Visceral metastases with or without lymph node metastases or with or without
bone metastases

Alkaline Phosphatase
o
ALP<ULN
o
ALP≥ULN
Note: Blood samples to measure ALP levels for stratification will be analyzed in a central
laboratory.
A computer-generated randomization list will be prepared by the Bayer Randomization
Manager. The randomization number will be used to link the subject to a treatment group and
to a medication package.
The Investigator (or designated associate) will obtain the randomization number and the
medication package numbers assigned to a subject by accessing the Interactive Voice/Web
Response System (IXRS) after confirming that the subject meets all the inclusion criteria and
does not meet any of the exclusion criteria.
An IXRS description and handbook will be provided to each investigational site.
7.4
Dosage and administration of study treatment
7.4.1
Dose modifications of study drug
The study drug will be administered as oral 300 mg tablets. The dose of study drug to be
administered is 600 mg (2 tablets of 300 mg) twice daily with food, equivalent to a total daily
dose of 1200 mg. Placebo matching darolutamide tablets in appearance will be administered
twice daily with food.
The dose or dosing schedule of the study drug may be modified following the occurrence of
clinically significant AEs. Doses of study drug may be delayed or reduced in case of clinically
significant toxicities that are considered by the Investigator to be related to study drug.
Toxicities will be graded using the National Cancer Institute-Common Terminology Criteria
for Adverse Events (NCI-CTCAE) v 4.03. All dose modifications regardless of relatedness
should be recorded on the eCRF. If a subject experiences several study drug-related toxicities
with different grading, the recommendation of the worst grading should be used.
